author: show-me state times
title: Missouri man admits to new child pornography charge while on supervised release
text:
A Missouri man residing in a halfway house after serving prison time for producing child pornography admitted on May 27 to being caught again with child sexual abuse material.
Joseph Trahan, 62, pleaded guilty to one count of possession of child pornography. According to court documents, in August 2025, Trahan was on supervised release and living at a halfway house when authorities learned he had an unauthorized electronic device and had been viewing child sexual abuse material. On August 6, 2025, Trahan’s probation officer met with him. An investigation revealed conversations between Trahan and another registered sex offender about sex with a child and the discovery of more than 600 images containing such material. Authorities also found that Trahan maintained unregistered accounts on TikTok and Instagram.
Trahan is scheduled for sentencing on September 9. Both the U.S. Attorney’s Office and his lawyer have agreed to recommend a sentence of ten years in prison.
In 2007, Trahan was convicted in St. Louis federal court for production of child pornography after videotaping himself engaged in sexual activity with a minor and distributing the recordings by mail for money. He received a sentence of over twenty-two years followed by lifetime supervised release.
The U.S. Probation Office and the Federal Bureau of Investigation investigated this case, which is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kyle Bateman and Sila Karacal.
This prosecution is part of Project Safe Childhood, an initiative launched by the Department of Justice in May 2006 aimed at combating online exploitation and abuse involving children through coordinated federal, state, and local efforts.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Missouri investigates and prosecutes federal crimes including offenses related to civil rights enforcement across its jurisdiction covering forty-nine counties; it operates under the United States Department of Justice using facilities such as the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse in St. Louis, according to its official website .
